paras: The killings of Jim Bell, Ben Russell and George W. Griffin took place on Wednesday night, October 31, 1888, in Van Zandt County, Texas, when four white men who had gone to arrest Russell on a misdemeanor charge shot him and two companions before, according to the reports, they could obey an order to raise their hands. Accounts disagreed on whether one, two or three of the Black men died, and friends of the dead claimed that the shooting was political. Three of the four white men were arrested, charged with murder and released on bond, and a wire dispatch carried the story across the country.

According to a Canton telegram to the Austin Weekly Statesman, a capias had been issued for Russell's arrest for disturbing the peace, which the wire called a misdemeanor. The same correspondent reported a claim that the white men had tried to get Russell to join the Union Labor party and that Russell had answered that he would vote the Democratic ticket.

Four white men, named in the dispatches as W. L. Hays (or Hayes), Sam Stanford, Claud Stanford and Will James, went to make the arrest and found Russell together with Bell and Griffin. The three men, all described as "colored," were called on to hold up their hands, and before they could comply they were fired on.

The Statesman reported Bell killed and Russell, George Washington and Tom Griffin mortally wounded, while the San Antonio Daily Light had Bell killed and Russell and "George W. Griffen" mortally wounded. The wire dispatch dated Canton, November 3, listed Bell, Russell and Griffin as killed. A Van Zandt County dispatch in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette two days later recalled that "two negroes were killed near Owlet Green" the previous Wednesday.

The first wire report said an investigation was being made, and the Statesman reported that officers were looking for the four men. According to the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, officers brought in the two Stanfords and William James on capiases charging them with the murder of Ben Russell and George Washington Jones, "both colored," while Hayes remained at large after officers chased him for a day and a night. The three waived an examining trial before County Judge J. S. Spinks and were jailed when they could not make bail, though a later item reported all three released on bond. No report of an inquest, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage, nor of the fate of the men described as mortally wounded.

The San Antonio Daily Light gave it one sentence in a "State News" column, adding that the killing was "said to be the result of politics," and the Statesman ran its telegram under "One Negro Killed and Three Mortally Wounded—Causes of the Affray." Outside Texas, the Canton dispatch appeared on November 3 in the Alexandria Gazette and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, whose headline read "Three Negroes Murdered." On November 4 it ran in the Richmond Dispatch, the Memphis Appeal and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, among others.

Most versions credited the political explanation to "friends of the dead men." A variant printed in Lancaster and in the Mitchell Capital in Dakota said instead that the men were killed in "a conspiracy" because they had refused to join "clubs formed against the Democracy." Headlines ranged from the Richmond Dispatch's plain "Three Men Killed" to the Omaha Bee's "A Political Quarrel Leads to the Murder of Three Men" and the St. Paul Daily Globe's "Texas Regulators Make Short Work of Three Negroes." The Mitchell Capital went furthest, running the story under "The Race War in the South" with the subhead "Three Negroes Wantonly Murdered by Deputies Sent to Arrest Them."

Of the conflicting death tolls, the Fort Worth Daily Gazette's is the latest and the only one drawn from the murder charges, and it named two dead men. The third victim's name also varied, from "George W. Griffin" in the wire to two men, George Washington and Tom Griffin, in the Statesman, and "George Washington Jones" in Fort Worth. Only the Mitchell Capital's headline called the four men deputies; the Statesman distinguished them from "the officers" who were looking for them.

reader.title: Killings of Jim Bell, Ben Russell and George W. Griffin
bases: Four white men who went to serve a capias on Russell shot him and two companions before they could raise their hands, and three of the four were then charged with murder (A4, A14, A12).

A group of four white men, acting on the pretext of serving an arrest warrant for disturbing the peace, shot down at least one and possibly three Black men before they could comply, and county officers charged them with murder (A14, A4, A12). It falls short of certain because the four may have held a deputy's authority to make the arrest (A17) and friends of the dead gave a political motive rather than a summary punishment (A14).

The wire (A4), an independent Canton special telegram (A14) and a separate Fort Worth report of the arrests (A12) agree that four named white men going to arrest Russell shot him and his companions, though they differ on the number of dead.

accounts.label: Wire report (Canton, Nov. 3)
accounts.gist: Bell, Russell and Griffin were killed when four men who went to arrest Russell on a misdemeanor met them, ordered hands up, and shot them before they could comply; friends claimed a political quarrel; an investigation was under way.

accounts.label: Wire variant ('conspiracy')
accounts.gist: Same facts, but friends claimed a conspiracy because the men had refused to join clubs formed against the Democracy and would vote the Democratic ticket.

accounts.label: Canton special telegram to the Statesman
accounts.gist: Bell was killed and Russell, George Washington and Tom Griffin mortally wounded; a capias for disturbing the peace was the occasion; it was claimed the white men had tried to get Russell to join the union labor party; officers were seeking the white men.

accounts.label: Fort Worth Gazette report of arrests
accounts.gist: Three of the four were brought in on capiases charging the murder of Ben Russell and George Washington Jones, waived examining trial, were jailed for want of bail and later released on bond; Hayes was at large.

framing.detail: Texas papers treated it as state news: one sentence in the San Antonio Light's 'State News' and the Statesman's 'One Negro Killed and Three Mortally Wounded—Causes of the Affray'.
Most out-of-state papers ran the wire under plain heads such as 'Three Men Killed' or 'Negroes Killed', with the political explanation attributed to friends of the dead.
The Mitchell Capital headed it 'The Race War in the South. Three Negroes Wantonly Murdered by Deputies Sent to Arrest Them', and other heads used 'Murdered' or 'Murder'.

conflicts.note: The Fort Worth report is the latest and comes from the murder charges themselves, which favors two dead by Nov. 4-5; the earlier Statesman and Light reports of mortal wounds may describe men who died afterward. The Owlet Green item (A13) matches in county, day and race but does not name the victims.
